summary: Keppel Island light at Port Saunders: the 1901 wooden tower, inactive since a 1992 skeletal light took over beside it; reached only by boat.

structures.type: square pyramidal wood tower with lantern and gallery
structures.note: The historic tower, painted with red and white horizontal bands (Rowlett); inactive since 1992 (Rowlett). LighthouseFriends: it first showed a fixed white sixth-order dioptric light, 32.6 m (107 ft) above high water.

structures.type: square skeleton tower with an octagonal lantern house
structures.note: Modern tower beside the historic one, carrying the working light (CCG list: Fl W 5s, focal height 36.5 m, range 11 nm). Built 1992 (LF; Rowlett).

staffing.status: staffed until 1989; fully automated light from 1992 (LF)

access.note: Reached only by boat. Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett).

facts.agency: Town of Port Saunders (station buildings); Canadian Coast Guard owns the land under the light (SaltWire, undated)

events.note: Tower built; the light was kerosene-burning when first built (Town; LF; Rowlett).
Station established; fixed white sixth-order dioptric light at 32.6 m (LF).
Kerosene light changed to a flashing white light fuelled by acetylene gas (LF).
Keeper's dwelling, fog alarm building and storage buildings built (LF).
Type F diaphone fog alarm, worked by compressed air from an oil engine, operating from September 1958 (LF).
Second dwelling built for an assistant keeper (LF).
Electronic fog signal replaced the diaphone; light converted to diesel-generated electricity (LF).
Modern skeletal tower erected beside the historic tower (LF; Rowlett).
Fully automated light erected; the station had been staffed until 1989 (LF).
Historic tower's light inactive; the new tower took over (Rowlett: 'Inactive since 1992').
Keeper's dwellings, three sheds and five acres placed on the market for $250,000 (LF; Rowlett).

keepers.name: Moses Lavers
keepers.note: LighthouseFriends keeper list gives 1950 to 1987. The LighthouseFriends text says he was appointed keeper of the new fog alarm (which began operating in September 1958), served nearly thirty years and retired in 1987; it calls him 'Keeper Laver' and gives no appointment year. See resolved_conflicts.

corrections.proposed: inactive (historic tower since 1992); the 1992 modern light is active
corrections.why: The historic wooden tower has been inactive since 1992 (Rowlett). The working light since 1992 is the modern skeletal tower beside it (CCG list; LighthouseFriends).

corrections.proposed: historic square pyramidal wood tower (1901; inactive since 1992) and a 1992 square skeleton tower, 11.3 m, active
corrections.why: The 11.3 m height in the CCG list belongs to the 1992 modern tower, not the historic tower the story is about. The record attributes it to the historic station.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Coast Guard list gives the working light as Fl W 5s at 36.5 m focal height, range 11 nm. The Lighthouse Directory has two entries: one gives focal plane 37 m with one second on and fifteen off, the other gives 17 m with a flash every 15 seconds. The Coast Guard list is used.

Both can be true: the historic tower has been inactive since 1992 (Rowlett), and the modern tower beside it shows the working light (CCG list). The record's 'Sources differ on whether the light is still lit' is resolved by separating the two towers.

LighthouseFriends and the Directory say the town owns the station buildings and acquired the station except the light tower. SaltWire (undated) says the lighthouse stands on land owned by the Coast Guard and that 25 acres of the island are Crown land. The buildings and the land under the light may have different owners; this is not settled here.

The LighthouseFriends keeper list gives 1950 to 1987. Its text says Lavers was appointed keeper of the new fog alarm, which began operating in September 1958, and served nearly thirty years, but it gives no appointment year. The first draft's 'in 1958' was an inference and is removed; the story gives the list's 1950 start and says the text does not explain it.

notes_for_editor: The Newfoundland House of Assembly journals for 1901, 1902 and 1903 returned HTTP 500 from dai.mun.ca, so the 1901 build and the early keepers rest on LighthouseFriends, the Directory and the Town page; check 1901-1903 when that host recovers. The Town's history page says the island was once a Spanish burial ground; no other source here says so and the story does not use it. The SaltWire column is undated and is a property piece; the agent named in it is not named here. The Directory's two modern-light entries disagree (37 m focal plane with 1 s on and 15 s off; 17 m focal height with a flash every 15 s); the Coast Guard list (Fl W 5s, 36.5 m) is used. LighthouseFriends gives the historic light's focal height as 32.6 m, which is not the modern light's figure. The 2013 price comes from LighthouseFriends and the Directory; the 2015 reduction and 2017 status from the Directory only. 'The Forgotten Bay' (Stuart L. Harvey, 1997), which LighthouseFriends cites, was not read. The keepers' family is not named in the story: LighthouseFriends prints the number of children and their school trips, and the story leaves them out. Moses Lavers is the LighthouseFriends roster name; the text calls him 'Keeper Laver'; they are the same entry. Not used: the Lighthouse Digest database entry and a lighthouse-index page, both aggregators. The Keppel Island 'lighthouse-old' id: the record's agency and ownership describe the station, so the corrections separate the historic tower from the 1992 tower.
